# Classical Mechanics

Classical mechanics describes the motion of macroscopic objects from projectiles to components of machinery, as well as astronomical objects such as spacecraft, planets, stars, and galaxies.

## Newton's Three Laws of Motion

The axiomatic foundation of classical mechanics consists of three physical laws:

| Law | Principle | Mathematical Formulation | Physical Interpretation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| First Law | Law of Inertia | $\sum \mathbf{F} = 0 \implies \frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = 0$ | A body remains at rest or constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force. |
| Second Law | Fundamental Law of Dynamics | $\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt} = m\mathbf{a}$ | The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass. |
| Third Law | Action-Reaction Symmetry | $\mathbf{F}_{A \to B} = -\mathbf{F}_{B \to A}$ | When one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body simultaneously exerts a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. |

## Universal Gravitation and Orbit Mechanics

Newton deduced the universal law of gravitation, stating that every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses:

$$
F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}
$$

When velocities approach the speed of light or scale shrinks to atomic dimensions, classical mechanics is superseded by relativistic dynamics and [[Physics/Quantum/Schrodinger|quantum wave mechanics]].
